appraisal_events.evidence: Through an œil-de-bœuf the narrator sees the baron « enchaîné sur un lit comme Prométhée sur son rocher », « déjà tout en sang, et couvert d'ecchymoses », beaten with a nail-studded martinet by Maurice, in a house he had had Jupien buy for him and where « tout le monde connaissait plus ou moins sa personnalité et son nom ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The passage lowers Charlus by staging the exact reverse of the discourse he has just delivered on the boulevards — Greek athletes, Spartan virility, the heroes of the war — and by making the narrator the unseen witness of his paid degradation.

appraisal_events.evidence: « Oui, nous nous sommes abîmés dans le dilettantisme, nous tous, vous aussi… vous pouvez faire comme moi votre mea culpa » ; the narrator beats his breast « par surprise du reproche, manque d'esprit de repartie, déférence », an answer he calls « parfaitement stupide car je n'avais pas l'ombre de dilettantisme à me reprocher ».
appraisal_events.explanation: Charlus's reproach lands and is accepted; the narrator records his own failure to answer as a defeat in the exchange, even though the baron's reasoning is described as absurd.

appraisal_events.evidence: Charlus takes the narrator « comme vague intermédiaire pour des ouvertures de paix » with Morel; and although the baron belongs to « une famille plus ancienne que les Capétiens », is rich and vainly sought after by elegant society while « Morel n'être rien », « encore était-ce Morel qui avait le dessus s'il ne voulait pas se rendre ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator's analysis explicitly reverses the two men's ranks in the affective contest: the absent, socially insignificant violinist holds the advantage over the baron, who needs him and falls back on hired resemblances to him.

status_effects.explanation: The passage's verdict on the baron collapses when his discourse of heroism and virility is answered by the sight of him bleeding and chained under a hired man's whip.

His standing falls inside the world of the passage: the staff of the house know his name and rank, nickname him « l'Homme enchaîné » and discuss the fifty francs he pays, so that his person is common talk among people far beneath him.
On the boulevards the baron keeps the upper hand in talk: he monologues unanswered and extracts a mea culpa from his listener.
He is the one who sues for peace through an intermediary, and all his advantages count for nothing against Morel's refusal.
He accepts a reproach he knows to be undeserved, having found no reply, and calls the capitulation stupid himself.
Absent from the scene, Morel nonetheless holds the leverage: his refusal governs, and it is Charlus who must send envoys.

ambiguities: The diminishment of Charlus is delivered by juxtaposition rather than comment, and the Promethean simile lends the flagellation scene a grandeur that cuts partly against the degradation, leaving the degree of narratorial endorsement open.
